analysis.one_liner: Extends child labor protections to children working on farms and raises penalties for violations.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a hearing and died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal child labor law has long treated farm work differently from other jobs: children as young as 12 could legally work unlimited hours on farms outside school hours, and 16-year-olds could do hazardous work that would be illegal for them anywhere else. This bill would have closed most of those gaps, raising the minimum age for hazardous farm work to 18, keeping the exception only for children working on their own parents' farms outside school hours, adding 100 labor inspectors, raising fines, and requiring employers to report serious injuries and deaths of workers under 18. It died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Children employed in agriculture, most of them from immigrant and low-income families, who would face a higher minimum age for dangerous work, fewer hours during school, pesticide protections, and a government that counts and investigates their injuries.

how_it_helps.text: Raises from 16 to 18 the minimum age for hazardous agricultural work and allows employment of children under 16 only on a parent's own farm and outside school hours.
Repeals the old waiver that had let 14- and 15-year-olds do hand-harvest work for wages.

Raises civil penalties for child labor violations from a $10,000 cap to up to $50,000, and up to $100,000 for repeated or willful violations causing serious injury or death, and creates prison time of up to five years for willful violations causing a child worker's death or permanent disability.

Requires the Labor Department to hire at least 100 more Wage and Hour Division inspectors and boosts prosecution budgets, and requires employers to report any serious injury, illness, or death of an agricultural worker under 18 within five days.
Folds federal pesticide-safety standards into the child labor rules and funds dropout-prevention programs for migrant and seasonal farmworker youth.

analysis.who_pays: Agricultural employers, who would face stricter age limits, larger fines, criminal exposure, mandatory injury reporting, and more frequent inspections.

drawbacks.text: The extra 100 inspectors and larger prosecution budget are only required 'subject to the availability of appropriations,' so Congress could have passed the bill and funded none of it.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the cost: farms, including small family operations that hire local teens, would bear higher compliance burdens and fines, and the 18-year hazardous-work limit would end paid work that some 16- and 17-year-olds currently rely on.
The bill does keep the family-farm exemption, so children working on their own parents' farms could still do hazardous work; it regulates commercial employers, not family farms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go to one of the least protected groups in the workforce — children doing dangerous farm work under rules written in 1938 — while the costs fall on the growers who employ them. The main design weakness is that the enforcement parts depend on future appropriations, so the paper protections could have gone unfunded. Still, on paper this was a targeted fix, not a broad mandate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, then to two of its subcommittees, and never got a hearing, a markups, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lucille Roybal-Allard introduced the CARE Act on July 27, 2005, with 15 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce the day it was introduced.
On October 12, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections and the Subcommittee on 21st Century Competitiveness.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no vote, and the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Agricultural employers came out ahead: they kept the looser child labor standards that allow children as young as 12 to work unlimited hours on farms and 16-year-olds to do hazardous work, and faced none of the higher fines, injury-reporting duties, or extra inspections. Child farmworkers remained under the 1938-era rules.

for.name: Rep. Lucille Roybal-Allard
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought cosponsors.

for.name: 15 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Rep. John Boehner
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired received the bill, referred it to subcommittees, and never held a hearing or markup on it, keeping it from the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 15 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-run committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Agricultural employers (farms and growers hiring minors)
industries.note: The bill raises the age limits for farm work, multiplies penalties up to $100,000, adds criminal exposure for deaths, and mandates injury reporting and more inspectors. Growers' interest in cheap, flexible juvenile labor sits directly against the safety of the children doing the work.
The bill guarantees at least $10 million a year in grants for dropout-prevention programs for farmworker youth, routed through the existing Workforce Investment Act system.
